metadata.title: The One Step No Script Can Skip.
metadata.subtitle: The m5-onboard Skill (Claude Code Plugins)
metadata.purpose: Take apart the m5-onboard skill: explain how one command chains detect, identify, flash, and install; name what native-USB hardware refuses to let software do; and judge the design choice to make the one un-automatable step loud rather than hidden. Land the carry-out that automation covers every stage but one — the button press stays a human's job, and no flag replaces it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. The script chains four stages — detect, identify, flash, install — behind one command. It automates every step it can reach in software. The one step it can't reach is a physical button, because on this board the USB hardware gives software no line to pulse. So: flash my board with one script — one exception?

beats.narration_text: Here's what one command actually does. onboard.py --apps buddy fires four stages in order. Detect opens a USB scan and picks up whatever port the operating system named the board — usbmodem on macOS, ttyACM or ttyUSB on Linux, COM on Windows — then reads back the chip identifier to confirm it's talking to real silicon, not a lookalike. Identify checks hardware signatures against known variants and offers a best-guess firmware match, but the final variant is always stated explicitly on the command line; the design refuses to auto-select, because a wrong guess boot-loops the device. Flash writes the firmware image. Install pushes the app bundle onto the freshly flashed board and reboots it. Two smaller tools exist for narrower jobs: pushing just the app bundle to a board that's already flashed, and running a post-flash hardware check. They optimized for one command that does the full chain, at the expense of any hands-off firmware guessing.

Three design realities collide once you actually run this. First, two board variants ship with the exact same USB signature, so nothing the script can read over USB will tell them apart — guess wrong on the command line and the board boot-loops. That's the reason identify doesn't auto-select; the protocol simply doesn't carry the answer. Second, a full run takes two to three minutes, so the script backgrounds itself and streams its output to a log file — because a silent terminal that just sits there for three minutes is indistinguishable from a crash, and a live tail keeps the operator honest. Third, the flash step itself: on boards that connect over native USB, there is no control line software can pulse to force the chip into flashing mode — no DTR, no RTS reaching the reset pin. So the script hands off to a physical dance. Hold the BOOT button, tap RESET while still holding, hold one more second, release. Then the script resumes. They optimized for one command at the expense of one hands-off run.

production_viz.label: THE BUTTON DANCE
production_viz.caption: the one step that needs a hand

beats.narration_text: That physical step is not universal — it's the price of one specific hardware choice. On native-USB boards the microcontroller speaks USB directly, and there is no side channel the host can drive into the reset pin; the classic software trick of toggling DTR and RTS is simply a no-op, because those lines don't exist as far as the chip is concerned. On boards that put a separate USB-to-serial bridge chip between the host and the microcontroller, the bridge exposes exactly those two control lines, and the flash tool pulses them straight into the reset and boot pins. Same script, same command — the button dance appears on one path and vanishes on the other, entirely because of which USB hardware happens to be sitting on the board. This design works if you value a board with fewer parts and lower cost; it fails if you need a run with no hands on it.
One script can detect, identify, flash, and install this board — every stage but one. The button press stays a human's job. No flag replaces a thumb.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm designing a Claude Code skill that automates flashing firmware and provisioning a class of embedded boards end-to-end from one command. Some of my target boards connect through a native-USB microcontroller and some through a USB-to-serial bridge chip. Explain exactly why the bridge-chip boards can be flashed with no human touch — how DTR and RTS toggling reaches the reset line — while native-USB boards need a physical button sequence to enter flashing mode, and what the standard hold-BOOT, tap-RESET, hold-one-second, release dance is actually doing at the chip level. Then design the skill's contract so the button-press requirement is loud instead of silent: what the skill should say before starting, what it should log while it waits, and what the failure mode should be if the human never presses the buttons. Go deeper: what would it cost — in extra hardware and bill-of-materials changes — to add a software-controlled reset line to a native-USB board so the whole flow could run hands-off, and at what production volume does that stop being worth it?
